title: First adversary argument: Scripture cannot prove Scripture, so the Church's testimony must
source_text: II. Primum ergo sic authoritatem Scripturae ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere, probare conantur. Scriptura, inquiunt, per Scripturam probari non potest. Ergo, ut de Scriptura apud fideles constet, necesse est ut sit testimonium aliquod divinum et infallibile, quo Scriptura probetur. Sed hoc testimonium aliud esse non potest quam Ecclesiae testimonium, quo in terris nullum est certius et augustius. Quod si dicas Scripturam multis in locis se divinam asserere, regerunt illi, ut Scripturae credamus se divinam asserenti, necesse esse ut de illius divinitate jam aliunde persuasi simus. Nec enim, ut scriptum aliquod pro divino habeatur, sufficit ut se divinum afferat: quod fecere libri plerique Apocryphi, qui merito tamen rejecti sunt. Et certe Scripturam per Scripturam ipsam probari non posse inde manifestum videtur, quod probatio omnis est a notioribus. At idem non est seipso notius et ignotius. Neque authoritatem Scripturae nescienti, aut de Scriptura dubitanti ex Scriptura quicquam probatur.
pass_a_gloss: First, therefore, they try to prove that the authority of Scripture depends on the authority of the Church. Scripture, they say, cannot be proved by Scripture. Therefore, in order that Scripture may be established among the faithful, it is necessary that there be some divine and infallible testimony by which Scripture is proved. But this testimony can be nothing other than the testimony of the Church, than which there is none more certain and august on earth. But if you say that Scripture in many places asserts itself to be divine, they retort that in order that we may believe Scripture asserting itself to be divine, it is necessary that we already be persuaded of its divinity from elsewhere. For it is not enough, for some writing to be held as divine, that it assert itself to be divine: which most of the Apocryphal books did, and yet were rightly rejected. And certainly that Scripture cannot be proved by Scripture itself seems manifest from this, that every proof is from things better known. But the same thing is not better known and less known than itself. Nor is anything proved from Scripture to one who does not know the authority of Scripture, or who doubts about Scripture.
pass_b_english: Their first attempt is to prove that Scripture's authority hangs on the Church's. Scripture, they say, cannot be proved by Scripture. So for the faithful to be sure of Scripture, some divine and infallible testimony must prove it. That testimony, they claim, can only be the Church's — none more certain or august on earth.

If you answer that Scripture in many places asserts its own divinity, they retort that we would already have to be persuaded of that divinity from elsewhere before we could believe the assertion. Mere self-claim is not enough: most of the Apocrypha claimed to be divine and were rightly rejected.

And it seems plain that Scripture cannot prove Scripture, because every proof moves from what is better known — and the same thing cannot be both better and less known than itself. Nothing from Scripture proves anything to someone who does not yet grant Scripture's authority, or who still doubts it.

choices.why: Keeps the solemn comparative of Church dignity.
